news.title: Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her? | Margaret Sullivan
news.text:
The moment that the world found out that Dolly Parton had died, I was in a hair salon in the reddest congressional district in New York state. The neighborhood on the shore of Lake Erie where I move every summer voted solidly for Donald Trump in 2024.

I often pass a lawn sign that has something misogynistic to say about New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, and the mere mention of Kamala Harris’s name can bring derisive jokes. Of course, there certainly are liberals and independents to be found, but on balance the area leans right.

On my errands around town, I’ve heard scornful comments about transgender people, and the local Catholic church where I sometimes attend mass has a priest who, during a homily this summer, praised Trump for his war in Iran.

A lot of the people I’ve chatted with around town are outspoken about being anti-vaccine.

But when cellphones started pinging with the news about Dolly, it’s not overstating things to say that everybody was devastated. Stylists and customers alike seemed to feel a personal connection – to her music, to her philanthropy, to her sheer goodness.

How did Dolly, a rags-to-riches country music superstar with a Tennessee twang and bedazzled everything, manage to endear herself to Americans of every political stripe?

What was her secret – and does it hold some wisdom for the those who seek unity in this divided nation, who appreciate civility, who believe there’s an American ethos that transcends our ugly politics?

Some of it, surely, was that she had a gift for poking fun at herself, and joining in the laughter, as when she would say she didn’t mind being called a dumb blonde because she knew, after all, that she wasn’t dumb – and that she wasn’t a blonde. After her illness made headlines last year, she took to social media to make a simple point: “I ain’t dead yet.” She called herself a “Backwoods Barbie” in a song of that name.

Then there was her remarkable generosity. Her organization, Imagination Library, gave more than 330m books to children around the world. She founded it, in part, she said, because her father couldn’t read or write.

She never forgot where she came from, as she raised money for a new hospital in her home country in Tennessee, or offered $500 awards to local teenagers when they graduated from high school.

Still, how did she manage not to alienate the Maga world when she promoted the Covid-19 vaccine (the research for which she had helped fund)?

Again, the humor helped, as when she changed the words of one of her most famous songs, Jolene to something that rhymed, and sang “vaccine, vaccine” in promotional videos. You had to smile, and maybe decide to get the jab, or at least to tolerate those who did. And she never made it political.

“She practiced a unique brand of radical acceptance,” wrote Jad Abumrad in a New York Times essay this week. “No one would ever be thrown out of the Big Dolly Tent.”

And, though she is being mourned as something of an angel on earth, she was a razor-sharp businessperson. She was smart and savvy about it all, as befitted the superstar who chalked up 25 No 1 country singles over the years.

As Abumrad learned while interviewing and observing her at length as he created the podcast Dolly Parton’s America, she always told her own story.

“If a male talkshow host made a joke about her figure, she’d make an ever better joke about it. She was always two steps ahead of you. She never allowed herself to be a part of a story of which she was not the author.”

Can what Dolly Parton did be bottled somehow? Can her serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity be sprinkled over our troubled waters to calm and soothe them?

Probably not – there is only one Dolly Parton – but that doesn’t mean we can’t learn something from this rare individual.

The rest of us might channel Dolly a bit more, and remember that a self-deprecating joke goes a long way toward easing tensions. We might recognize that financial success need not turn into ego glorification or arrogance.

And most of all, we might keep in mind that genuine generosity – if it comes from the heart – has the power to transcend politics.

Dolly Parton’s legacy, of course, resides in her wonderful songs, from Coat of Many Colors to 9 to 5. That’s what she would want.

But I don’t think she’d object if we also kept in mind her authentic kindness, her disarming wit – and the “radical acceptance” that fueled it all.

 Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

news.title: Trump Drops Plans to Attend 25th Anniversary 9/11 Ceremony at Ground Zero
news.text:
Donald Trump is reportedly set to skip the Ground Zero commemorations in New York marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

The president, a New York native who built his real estate brand in the city, has been a familiar presence at 9/11 memorial events over the years.

But in 2026, he is expected to honor the victims for the second year in a row at a Pentagon remembrance ceremony after being denied a speaking role at the New York event, according to The New York Times.

Trump had sought to deliver remarks at the National September 11 Memorial and Museum, and his aides had reportedly conducted advance planning visits ahead of the anniversary.

Sources told the outlet that organizers at the museum are determined to keep the solemn ceremony free from partisan politics, noting that elected officials have not been permitted to speak there since 2012.

Vice President JD Vance is expected to attend the New York 9/11 memorial ceremony on behalf of the Trump administration, while former Presidents Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and George W. Bush are also anticipated to be there.

Trump is scheduled to return to Washington after attending the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Texas two days before September 11.

As he did the previous year, Trump is expected to speak at the Pentagon’s September 11 ceremony, where political leaders are still allowed to deliver addresses.

He will then leave the country for Ireland to visit his golf course where the Irish Open is being held.

His flight would be significantly easier on local air traffic going out of Joint Base Andrews in Maryland than from any of the New York-area airports. 

In a statement to the Times, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly emphasized a remembrance of the victims but made no reference to the President’s specific plans. 

Our News Outlet has reached out to the White House for further comment. 

MORE STORY: Why America’s $40 Trillion Debt Won’t Trigger Fiscal Doom

The President also commemorated September 11 at the Pentagon last year, in a ceremony that was moved into the internal courtyard after the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

Trump pledged to always honor those who died on that day. 

‘We will defend the nation they served, the values they upheld and the freedom for which they died,’ he said. 

‘We will support our troops, we will protect our families, and we will preserve the American way of life for every future generation.

‘We will build taller, grow stronger, fight harder and soar higher, and together we will go forward as one people with one heart, one faith, one flag and one glorious destiny under almighty God,’ he added.

Trump did go to New York afterward, as he attended a Major League Baseball game between the New York Yankees and Detroit Tigers at Yankee Stadium. 

The last time Trump attended the Ground Zero ceremony was in 2024, when he was in the same company as Kamala Harris, as the two shared an awkward handshake. 

Trump and Harris appeared cordial at Ground Zero as they met for a second time in 24 hours following the first debate between the two, even sharing the handshake which was facilitated by Republican-turned-Democratic former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg.

Harris stood alongside President Joe Biden during the ceremony while Bloomberg acted as a buffer separating the current administration from Trump and his running mate Vance. Trump allegedly complimented Harris’s debate performance.

The attendance by Trump, Biden and Harris is rare and marks one of the few times the former president and current president have been in the same space.

The three would not be in the same space again until Trump’s second inauguration in Washington just four months later.

news.text:
U.S. presidents and politicians who have given speeches on the Sept. 11 anniversary in years past have either done so at the Pentagon, from the White House, or in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, where the fourth plane crashed in 2001.

In 2025, President Trump spent the anniversary of the terrorist attack at the Pentagon ceremony, in which he both led a wreath-laying ceremony and delivered remarks reflecting on those who died and acted heroically during attack.

In 2024, then-Presidential candidate Trump attended the memorial ceremony at Ground Zero in Manhattan alongside then-Senator JD Vance, while former Vice President Kamala Harris attended the ceremony alongside then-President Joe Biden.

Two planes hit each of the World Trade Center buildings in lower Manhattan, while one plane hit the Pentagon. The plane that crashed in Shanksville was diverted from the terrorists’ suspected target of Washington, D.C., as patrons aboard the flight fought back against the al-Qaeda terrorists on the plane.

news.title: Democrats Try to Brush Aside 'Woke 1'
news.text:
"'Woke 1' was crazy." So said Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) on ABC News' "This Week" earlier this month. 

She said she was quoting New York City Councilman Chi Osse, whom The New York Times characterizes as "far left." This was where Ocasio-Cortez seemed to be located on the ideological spectrum after her surprise defeat of House Democratic leadership member Joseph Crowley in the 2018 Democratic primary. 

At that time, she was a 28-year-old former waitress and organizer for Sen. Bernie Sanders' (I-Vt.) 2016 presidential campaign. Today, a decade later, she's a nationally known figure often mentioned as a presidential candidate. In polls for the 2028 nomination, she ranks fourth in the RealClearPolitics average, behind 2024 nominee and former Vice President Kamala Harris, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.), and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and Polymarket places her odds of winning as better than any of theirs. 

As a possible national candidate, Ocasio-Cortez obviously has a motive to brush aside, as she did with a charmingly self-deprecatory laugh, the exotic positions she and other Democrats took on issues, particularly after the death of George Floyd in May 2020 and the ensuing multicity violent rioting. 

They included demands to "defund the police" or even abolish police departments, to step up the already institutionalized demands for "diversity, equity and inclusion" hiring, and promotions in bureaucracies, public and private, for racial reparations. These weren't just words: Cities such as New York, San Francisco, Chicago, and Minneapolis did hustle to partially defund their police departments. 

The Floyd riots and calls for defunding police were immediately followed by a sharp spike upward in violent crime. Liberals have characterized that spike as a response to COVID-19, but charts compiled by writer Steve Sailer make it clear that the spike began not with the lockdowns but with the riots and Woke 1 depolicing. 

At the same time, the lockdowns, enforced with Woke 1 censoriousness, were causing not just economic damage but also long-lasting harm to children who were kept out of teacher union-run schools long after it was clear children were not vectors of the virus. And Woke 1 transgender demands, for biological men on women's sports teams and public financing of even pre-adults' gender transition surgery, were advanced by the Biden administration and endorsed by Harris. 

Now there are numerous signs that the nation is putting Woke 1 so far in the rearview mirror as to be invisible and has little appetite for Woke 2. Items include: 

— The lack of visible vehement protests at the elimination of DEI programs, racial quotas and preferences, in federal regulations, in many state and local governments, and even in their strongholds in the universities. You hear grumbling about the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, but nothing like the politically charged attacks on its 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade. There's covert opposition and attempts to retain DEI under different labels, but you don't hear Democratic candidates talking about the issue. 

— Similarly, there's a dog-who-didn't-bark response to the Trump administration's effective shutdown of illegal immigration on the southern border. Missing from the political dialogue have been media stories about the asylum-seekers who are obliged now to pursue their claims not from somewhere in the continental United States but from a not particularly helpful or sympathetic Mexico or somewhere even more distant. 

— Violent crime rates seem sharply down. After the Floyd riots, homicides rose even more in 2021 and seemed on a trajectory to reverse all the enormous progress in crime reduction accomplished since the reforms pioneered by former Mayor Rudy Giuliani in New York in the 1990s. Homicides declined in 2025 to below the lowest numbers of the post-Giuliani years, and the FBI reported that violent crime dropped 9.3 percent, the biggest drop since 1936. For 2026, statistics aren't fully available, but there are starkly lower rates of violent crime in New York, and Baltimore has seen a huge drop in homicides in the 2020s. Why the huge drop in violent crime? No one is sure, but it comes as Democratic politicians are hastening to assure us that they never actually really wanted to abolish the police and the prisons when they were saying so back in Woke 1. 

— The revelations of the hypocrisy and lies of Dr. Anthony Fauci and other public health officials during the COVID-19 epidemic. Fauci, who, according to his diaries, delighted in partying with Washington elites, had to sit mute and invoke the Fifth Amendment as he was credibly attacked for having misled the public. Masking, he admitted privately, didn't prevent the spread of disease, even as he urged penalties for non-maskers. The vaccine, while reducing deaths, did not prevent transmission, as he had assured the nation. Fauci's efforts to discredit as "a conspiracy theory" the argument that the virus spread from a leak from the Wuhan laboratory he financed increasingly look very much like an effort to cover up the evidence that he financed the lab's gain-of-function research surreptitiously, to make the virus more dangerous, in violation of a presidential order. The initial order, by the way, came from former President Barack Obama, not President Donald Trump. 

Against this evidence of the discrediting of Woke 1, come recent victories and near victories of members of, or sympathizers with, the Democratic Socialists of America, whose platform calls for the abolition of police and prisons. Those candidates have been emphasizing economic issues, however, which pass muster in Democratic primaries but may not in general electorates in states such as Michigan. 

What is not apparent in the political landscape is nostalgia for Woke 1 police defunding, for heavy-handed statism like Fauci's COVID-19 regime, or for a revival of the Biden administration's open-borders immigration policy. Democrats may be able to capitalize on the current Trump slump this year. But for 2028, they may not be able to dismiss questions about Woke 1 and Woke 2 as flippantly as Ocasio-Cortez tried to do this month.

news.title: Trump plans to mark 9/11 at the Pentagon, not Ground Zero
news.text:
NEW YORK – President Donald Trump is not planning to attend a ceremony in New York for the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center, in part because he wanted to deliver a speech and the annual event has long barred remarks, according to four people with knowledge of the events.

Trump’s team had conducted advance visits at the site and had initially signalled to officials in New York and in Washington that he intended to visit the memorial space known as Ground Zero, two of the people with knowledge of the events said.

The President’s interest in speaking on 9/11 was conveyed to memorial planners in recent weeks, three of the people with knowledge of the events said. But since 2012, politicians have been barred from speaking at the site.

The National September 11 Memorial & Museum, which oversees the site, has worked rigorously to keep the venue non-partisan and focused on the solemnity of the day.

Trump, a native New Yorker who talked often about the 9/11 attacks during his 2016 presidential campaign, is now expected to commemorate them at the Pentagon, two of the people with knowledge of the events said. The Pentagon also came under attack on 9/11.

Vice-President J.D. Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.

The President will go to the Pentagon after he attends a mid-term political convention in Texas. Officials have discussed some kind of tribute to the terrorist attack victims during that convention, which takes place Sept 9 and 10.

There are other considerations that led to Trump honouring the day in Washington, including that he will depart the next day for his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, where the Irish Open tournament will take place.

Leaving from John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City, or from Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, would snarl air and motor traffic to a much greater extent than with Trump leaving from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

Trump last attended the ceremony at Ground Zero in 2024, when he stood alongside Vance, former mayor Michael Bloomberg, president Joe Biden and vice-president Kamala Harris.

None of the officials made formal remarks. Trump visited a fire station in New York City after the event.

The 2026 anniversary marks a quarter-century since the worst attack on the United States after the assault on Pearl Harbor.

Anna Kelly, a spokesperson for the White House, did not address the President’s plans in a response to an e-mail seeking comment.

“On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honour their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans,” she said.

At the Pentagon, Trump will be allowed to speak, as he did in 2025 when he attended the remembrances there.

His speech that day came less than 24 hours after conservative activist Charlie Kirk, whose efforts to draw college-age voters into the MAGA movement were seen as significant to Trump’s 2024 victory, was shot and killed while speaking on a campus in Utah.

The ceremony had been intended to be held in a different spot that day but was moved to a new one amid security concerns about Trump after Kirk was assassinated.

“We recall the light of America’s best and bravest and the love that they showed in their final moments,” Trump said at the time.

“In their memory, we make a solemn pledge and a noble promise. We will honour always our great heroes, and you are our heroes.”

Trump has faced two assassination attempts and other murder-for-hire plots by alleged Iranian proxies. He has faced an uptick in threats since he began a war against Iran on Feb 28.

The 2026 event in Manhattan is expected to include former mayor Rudy Giuliani; former president Bill Clinton and his wife Hillary; former president George W. Bush and his wife Laura; and former president Barack Obama, among others, according to several people who have been close to the planning.

In the first decade after 9/11, elected officials would read poems and historic American documents, like the Gettysburg Address, at the ceremony.

But since 2012, the memorial has barred any speeches by politicians. Instead, politicians stand alongside their peers from opposing parties as families step onto a stage to read the names of the dead over the course of hours.

Trump’s advisers have discussed possibly taking federal control of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, including as recently as in 2025. Families of the Sept 11 victims have in recent years criticised the site over its leadership and finances.

Trump, who was in New York on the day of the attacks, spoke to a New Jersey television station in the aftermath, saying that a building he owned had gained in stature because the twin towers had fallen.

That building, 40 Wall Street, “actually was the second tallest building in downtown Manhattan, and it was actually – before the World Trade Center – was the tallest”.

He went on: “And then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest. And now it’s the tallest.” (The statement was not correct; 70 Pine Street, nearby, was taller than Trump’s building.) NYTIMES

news.title: Wisconsin GOP governor hopeful Tom Tiffany dismisses Trump’s Lake America renaming
news.text:
His remarks come hours after Trump signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” amid the Trump administration’s escalating trade war with Canada.

After trade negotiations between Canada and the United States collapsed last Friday, the Trump administration’s 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods hit the northern neighbor. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney counterpunched with “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory tariffs, saying Canada was “attacked” by the U.S.

As tensions heightened over the reciprocal levies, Trump first threatened on Truth Social to change the name of the lake between New York and Ontario on Tuesday. Then on Thursday, he made the name change a reality, implementing the measure for the U.S. government.

Carney made it clear his government would not be following the U.S.’s lead, saying in response that Canadians “know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

Tiffany is running in the “toss-up” gubernatorial race against the Democratic candidate, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who defied much of the polling expectations in the Democratic primary to defeat socialist state Rep. Francesca Hong.

TRUMP SIGNED AN ORDER TO RENAME LAKE ONTARIO TO LAKE AMERICA — WHAT TO KNOW

Limited polling on the Tiffany-Crowley matchup has shown Crowley up by single digits.

Trump flipped Wisconsin in 2024, beating former Vice President Kamala Harris in the Badger State by less than a point.

news.title: Three Undocumented Immigrants Arrested in Major Virginia Child Exploitation Sting Released on Bond
news.text:
Three of the nine men arrested in a Virginia child exploitation operation are illegal aliens with extensive criminal records, the Department of Homeland Security told Fox News. All three have since been released on bond.

Fairfax County police said Wednesday that the suspects allegedly went to the county intending to meet minors for sexual encounters after exchanging sexually explicit online messages with undercover detectives posing as juveniles.

DHS identified the three men as Reyben Leono Sanchez Hernandez, 21, of El Salvador; Wilmer Alexander Aguilar Cruz, 28, of El Salvador; and Henry Adalberto Flores Herrera, 39.

According to DHS, all three had previously been caught entering the United States illegally and were later released during the Obama administration. The department criticized the administration’s immigration policies as well as Fairfax County’s “sanctuary” policies, saying they contributed to what it characterized as an influx of criminal illegal aliens.

DHS said Sanchez Hernandez’s prior criminal history includes solicitation of prostitution from a minor. Fairfax County police also said he was charged with driving on a suspended license.

Officials said Sanchez Hernandez was apprehended near the Rio Grande Valley on Sept. 25, 2013, after illegally entering the United States. He was released into the country roughly a month later, according to DHS.

ICE lodged a detainer for Sanchez Hernandez with the Fairfax County Detention Center on July 29, officials said. Police said he has nevertheless been released on a $3,000 secured bond.

Aguilar Cruz was caught by Border Patrol near Hidalgo, Texas, in late 2012 before being released into the country during the Obama administration about two weeks later, according to DHS.

His criminal history includes allegations involving computer solicitation of a child, indecent liberties, proposed sex acts, sodomy, extortion and threats to burn, DHS said.

On April 27, 2019, police in Prince William County, Virginia, arrested Aguilar Cruz on charges of threatening to bomb or burn and making a threat in writing. ICE arrested him two days later, and he was released on bond on Aug. 9, 2019, according to DHS.

ICE placed a detainer on Aguilar Cruz with the Fairfax County Detention Center July 31, officials said. However, local police said he has since been released on $3,000 secured bond.

Flores Herrera’s criminal history includes felony solicitation of prostitution from a minor, sexual exploitation of a minor, driving under the influence of liquor and a traffic offense, according to DHS.

ICE placed a detainer on Flores Herrera with the Fairfax County Detention Center July 17, officials said. He has since been released on $5,000 secured bond.

DHS did not disclose how Flores Herrera entered the country.

A DHS spokesperson blamed former presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris for policies the department said paved the way for millions of unvetted illegal aliens to enter the U.S.

“These criminal illegal aliens were hand-delivered to Fairfax County communities by President Obama, who, like Sleepy Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, unleashed millions of unvetted illegal aliens into American communities and abused the law to do so,” the spokesperson said.

“President Trump and Secretary Mullin are now enforcing the law, arresting illegal aliens who have no right to be in our country and have reversed Democrats’ deadly catch and release policy.”

The department also urged Democratic Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger to increase cooperation with ICE to turn over detained immigrants.

“Under Governor Spanberger, Virginia has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime. During her first days in office, Governor Spanberger signed executive orders banning state cooperation with ICE as well as terminating 287(g) state and local agreements,” the department said. 

“We are urging Governor Spanberger to put her community first and turn over this criminal illegal alien to ICE.”

news.title: GOP Gov: Biden Weighed Trump Pardon in Jill Pillow Talk
news.text:
Joe Biden privately weighed the extraordinary idea of pardoning Donald Trump during a late-night conversation with first lady Jill Biden, according to Republican Utah Gov. Spencer Cox.

Cox recounts the exchange in his forthcoming book, an episode highlighted Thursday by The Atlantic, saying he raised the prospect of a Trump pardon with Biden in August 2023 — and was surprised to learn the president and first lady had already discussed it.

“Mr. President, I know this might sound crazy, but I think you should pardon Donald Trump,” Cox recalled telling Biden as they rode together in the presidential limousine in Salt Lake City.

Biden, Cox wrote, did not dismiss the suggestion. Instead, he replied: “You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while.”

“In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it,” Biden reportedly continued, acknowledging that many Americans were “demanding justice” even as he contemplated whether a pardon for Trump could serve a broader purpose.

The conversation came only days after Trump was federally indicted over his alleged attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

At that point, Trump was also already facing federal charges tied to his alleged mishandling of classified documents and was navigating his Manhattan case over alleged falsification of business records.

Cox, who was not backing Trump’s 2024 comeback bid at the time, said he worried that putting the 45th president on trial would further inflame the nation’s already volatile political climate.

He argued that by pardoning Trump, Biden could deescalate tensions and break the cycle of partisan retribution.

Biden, who granted 80 pardons, including to his son, Hunter, and former COVID czar Anthony Fauci, did not end up issuing one to Trump. 

It’s unclear if Jill dissuaded her husband from pardoning Trump. The first lady reportedly wielded significant political influence during her aging husband’s only term in office. 

A few days after Cox pitched the idea to Biden, Trump was indicted on state charges in Georgia over his alleged efforts to interfere in the presidential election in the Peach State. 

A presidential pardon would not have prevented prosecution in the Georgia or Manhattan cases. 

The federal cases against Trump, as well as the Georgia case, were dismissed after he defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. 

Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts at the end of his Manhattan trial. 

A spokesperson for Biden did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment. 

A few months before his conversation with Cox, Biden was asked by Fox News reporter Peter Doocy about potentially pardoning Trump. 

Biden cracked a smile and waved the question off, before replying, “I’ll see you guys” and calling it “a great question.”

news.title: Joe Biden considered pardoning Trump during 2023 pillow talk with Jill, GOP governor says
news.text:
Joe Biden discussed the possibility of granting President Trump a pardon in a bedtime conversation with his wife, Jill, according to Republican Utah Gov. Spencer Cox. 

In an anecdote from his upcoming book, detailed in The Atlantic Thursday, the governor revealed that he pitched Biden on the idea of pardoning Trump back in August 2023 — only to find out that the then-president and first lady had already been mulling it. 

“Mr. President, I know this might sound crazy, but I think you should pardon Donald Trump,” Cox recalled telling Biden, as the two sat inside the presidential limousine in Salt Lake City. 

According to the governor, Biden responded: “You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while.”

“In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it,” Biden continued, noting people were “demanding justice” but he was entertaining the idea of a Trump pardon. 

Just days before their conversation, Trump was hit with a federal indictment related to his alleged effort to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

Trump had already been facing federal charges for allegedly mishandling classified documents and was in the middle of his Manhattan trial for allegedly falsifying business records. 

Cox, who at the time was not supporting Trump’s re-election bid, feared that prosecuting the 45th president would intensify the political turmoil in the country.He argued that by pardoning Trump, Biden could deescalate tensions and break the cycle of partisan retribution.

Biden, who granted 80 pardons, including to his son, Hunter, and former COVID czar Anthony Fauci, did not end up issuing one to Trump. 

It’s unclear if Jill dissuaded her husband from pardoning Trump. The first lady reportedly wielded significant political influence during her aging husband’s only term in office. 

A few days after Cox pitched the idea to Biden, Trump was indicted on state charges in Georgia over his alleged efforts to interfere in the presidential election in the Peach State. 

A presidential pardon would not have prevented prosecution in the Georgia or Manhattan cases. 

The federal cases against Trump, as well as the Georgia case, were dismissed after he defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. 

Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts at the end of his Manhattan trial. 

A spokesperson for Biden did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment. 

A few months before his conversation with Cox, Biden was asked by Fox News reporter Peter Doocy about potentially pardoning Trump. 

Biden cracked a smile and waved the question off, before replying, “I’ll see you guys” and calling it “a great question.”
news.summary: "You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while. In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it,” Biden reportedly said.
news.author: Victor Nava

news.title: Biden Weighed Trump Pardon Idea as White House Pushes Back
news.text:
Joe Biden reportedly weighed the extraordinary possibility of issuing a presidential pardon for Donald Trump during the final stretch of his time in office, a revelation the White House argues underscores claims that Democrats had turned the Justice Department into a political weapon.

Before departing the presidency, Biden granted pardons to a number of high-profile figures close to him or connected to his administration, including his son Hunter Biden, Dr. Anthony Fauci and members of the House committee that investigated the January 6 Capitol attack.

But Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, a moderate Republican who did not endorse Trump until after the assassination attempt against him in Pennsylvania, said he was taken aback to hear that Biden had also been contemplating clemency for his predecessor.

Cox told The Atlantic that Biden raised the idea during an August 2023 phone call, well before the governor had thrown his support behind Trump. “You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while,” Cox recalled Biden saying.

According to Cox, Biden added that the subject had come up privately at home: “In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it.”

The Trump administration seized on the account, saying it demonstrated that Biden and his team understood Trump was facing unfair treatment but chose not to intervene.

“This shows President Biden knew he and his fellow extreme Democrats had weaponized the justice system against his political opponent, but did nothing to stop it,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Our News Outlet.

Bis then added a sharply sarcastic aside: “A real profile in courage.”

Cox believed that pardoning Trump from the criminal charges he faced in multiple states would help heal the nation and stop what he saw as a cycle of partisan revenge tactics. 

Biden told Cox that he was going to seriously consider the pardon – which Cox phrased to the President as something that ‘might sound crazy’ – despite his base ‘demanding justice’ for Trump. 

However, the clemency never came after Trump defeated Vice President Kamala Harris following Biden’s decision to not seek reelection.

Cox said he ‘hoped [Biden] would choose mercy over escalation’ by offering forgiveness to Trump.

Similarly, he asked Trump to unite the country following the shooting in Butler in August of 2024 and ‘hoped he would choose unity over retaliation.’

‘In both cases, things didn’t turn out quite the way I’d hoped,’ Cox said. 

Biden sparked fury on his way out the door by issuing preemptive pardons for his son Hunter, Dr Anthony Fauci and all nine members of the January 6 Committee.

The first pardon Biden issued after losing the 2024 presidential election to Trump was for Hunter, 54, who was convicted on felony tax charges as well as federal crimes for lying in 2018 about his drug use on a form to purchase a firearm.

This came to the ire of Democrats who felt it would give Trump permission to issue sweeping pardons without fear of being accused of hypocrisy.

And the same day Biden pardoned his son, Trump announced he would pardon January 6 defendants who were charged with crimes related to the Capitol attack.

Biden wrote in his pardon announcement that the action was warranted because they are public servants who have ‘been threatened with criminal prosecutions.’

‘These public servants have served our nation with honor and distinction and do not deserve to be the targets of unjustified and politically motivated prosecutions,’ he noted.

The 82-year-old Democrat also used his final moments in the Oval Office to give blanket protection to former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Mark Milley, who Trump has said deserves to be executed.

In all, the Biden administration granted more than 1,500 individuals clemency during his final weeks in the White House. 

Emails show Biden formally decided on issuing pre-emptive pardons for his family on January 19, 2024. 

Among the most controversial of all Biden’s pardons so far is the protection of Fauci from federal prosecution. 

He also got massive backlash for pardoning his own son from his federal crimes.

Biden wrote in a statement on the pardons: ‘Our nation relies on dedicated, selfless public servants every day. They are the lifeblood of our democracy. Yet alarmingly, public servants have been subjected to ongoing threats and intimidation for faithfully discharging their duties.’

news.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Nods Toward 2028 Run as She Rejoins DSA
news.text: Although U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) has long been one of the most well-known elected officials affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), her membership in the organization lapsed in 2019 and went unrenewed until August, the group said this week. The renewal comes as the New York lawmaker has drawn attention as a potential Democratic contender for the 2028 presidential election. Her confirmed membership also comes as progressive and democratic socialist candidates have recorded a series of high-profile victories ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, underscoring the progressive flank’s growing appeal for Democratic voters. This summer, New York DSA-backed candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier won congressional primaries, while other progressive candidates, like Melat Kiros, scored notable victories in races across the country. The timing of the renewal has some fueled speculation about Ocasio-Cortez's political future, particularly as discussions about the 2028 presidential race begin to ramp up. DSA said in a statement obtained by City & State New York, “While it is atypical for DSA to address the membership status of individuals, ongoing discussions about the 2028 presidential campaign have prompted this release.” In mid-August, Ocasio-Cortez told Jonathan Karl on ABC’s This Week that she was a member of the New York City DSA chapter, not the national DSA organization. Matt Klink, owner and president of Klink Campaigns, told Newsweek in an email, "The timing of her renewal, right as various DSA chapters float her for 2028 and the national organization gears up its endorsement process isn't a coincidence. It's a rebrand." He continued, "AOC realizes that her lane to the nomination begins in the far left lane. Nothing clarifies priorities like a presidential calendar." Newsweek has reached out to Ocasio-Cortez’s press team as well as the national DSA and New York chapters for comment via email on Thursday. Status of AOC’s DSA Membership Ocasio-Cortez signed up for a one-year national DSA membership in 2018 as she mounted her first bid for Congress. Her annual membership expired the following year and it was not renewed until just recently. At that time, memberships had to be renewed manually. Now, the DSA national chapter offers monthly memberships from $5 to $50 a month, or annual fees from $27 to $200. In a statement to DSA members that was then shared with City & State New York, the DSA said Ocasio-Cortez's membership had expired several years earlier: “Previously, the representative joined DSA in 2018 with a one-year membership, which DSA’s national leadership recently noticed had lapsed, in 2019. She has since renewed her membership as of this month.” They added that she is “in good standing of our organization.” The DSA has repeatedly referred to her as a member throughout those seven years, highlighting her 2020 reelection by referring to her as a “DSA member” in an X post and in a 2024 post, describing her and then-Representative Cori Bush as “DSA members.” In an August 9 interview with Karl, he asked Ocasio-Cortez if she was still a DSA member, which she replied, “of the New York City chapter. Yes.” She added, “So, every DSA chapter is formed locally. And so, the New York City DSA chapter, those are folks that you know. It’s my—it’s kind of like your local union chapter.” Klink told Newsweek that Ocasio-Cortez got "caught" claiming the affiliation, and the ABC interview "made the lapse impossible to explain away." He added, "AOC's socialist brand suggests the 'membership' was more useful as a label than a commitment." The DSA's national organization establishes the group's overall political direction, while its local chapters maintain some autonomy and organize campaigns and make decisions that may not always align with the national body. The DSA's national leadership withdrew its conditional endorsement of Ocasio-Cortez in 2024, citing disagreements over expectations and issues related to Israel and the Palestinian territories. According to the New York City DSA site, in order to be a "full, voting member of DSA nationally, you must join and pay dues with our national organization." It notes that 20 percent of national dues go back to the chapter. Whereas local dues "directly fund the work of our chapter, and are a 100% contribution to NYC-DSA, an entirely member-funded organization." The national group says it has over 100,000 members and chapters in every state. AOC Egg Freezing Sparks Speculation Earlier this month Ocasio-Cortez announced she is freezing her eggs, prompting a public conversation about cost, age, reproductive autonomy and what egg freezing can offer women. "This is a choice that I am making to feel more in control of my life," she said on Instagram in August about the process. The congresswoman added that she had been saving for the procedure for a long time. Ocasio-Cortez, who plans to document the process online, has shared videos of herself administering the hormone injections involved in preparing for egg retrieval. In her posts, the 36-year-old said women are often not given enough information about their bodies and reproductive health, including on fertility, pregnancy or menopause. Her decision, which has drawn praise and criticism, is one that has become increasingly common, with U.S. data showing that planned elective egg-freezing cycles have risen sharply over the past decade—even as many people who freeze their eggs do not return to use them within the first several years. In her announcement, she said, “Men run for office, or frankly they interview for jobs, and people don’t think in the back of their minds, ‘OK, this guy’s running for office, how old is he? Oh, well, is he going to want to start a family?’” she said. Some commentators have linked her decision to ongoing speculation about Ocasio-Cortez's political future, including a possible bid for president or Senate in 2028. What Has AOC Said About Running for President? Ocasio-Cortez has not publicly announced plans to run for president in 2028, though she recently left the door open to a White House bid, telling Karl, “I haven't ruled out the possibility.” She added, “I'm very humbled by the tremendous amount of support out there. I think that we have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations or plans.” When Karl followed up asking if she would run for Senate against Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, she said, “I think that anything is possible at this juncture.” As one of the most prominent voices on the Democratic Party's left flank, she is often cited as a potential future presidential candidate. Following Ocasio-Cortez's renewal of her DSA membership, a group of members launched an effort encouraging a future presidential bid. The X account DSA for AOC described itself as "DSA members organizing to seize the moment, unite Labor and the Left, and elect Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to the Presidency.” As of Thursday afternoon, about 1,100 people have signed a petition for her to become the DSA presidential nominee in 2028. However, not all DSA members have welcomed a potential Ocasio-Cortez presidential run. Red Star, a DSA caucus, published a statement expressing skepticism about backing a hypothetical Ocasio-Cortez campaign and questioning her alignment with some of the group's priorities. The group said in a July statement, "Red Star has serious doubts about throwing our weight behind an AOC presidential run," arguing she has a "lack of political and practical alignment with DSA." The group added, "This tension between DSA and AOC on political strategy has come up numerous times since her initial election to Congress in 2018, particularly vis-à-vis the struggle for Palestinian liberation." A July report by City & State New York detailed an internal DSA dispute over how the organization would handle a possible 2028 presidential endorsement, including whether DSA should conduct an all-member poll and who would ultimately make an endorsement decision. The publication reported that the procedural debate was driven in part by members' differing views of a potential Ocasio-Cortez candidacy. What Polls Show About AOC's 2028 Presidential Chances Ocasio-Cortez has appeared in early polling of potential Democratic contenders for the 2028 presidential nomination. An August Echelon Insights survey of 457 likely Democratic primary voters found Ocasio-Cortez at 11 percent, behind former Vice President Kamala Harris at 18 percent, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg with 13 percent and California Governor Gavin Newsom with 12 percent. The larger poll of 1,002 registered voters found her with a 33 percent favorability rating. The survey was conducted from August 13 to August 17 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. A June Economist/YouGov poll of 1,606 people also found her with a 33 percent favorability mark. That poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points. An Emerson College poll conducted on July 19 and July 20 put Ocasio-Cortez at 13 percent, tied for with Senator Jon Ossoff. Newsom and Buttigieg led both congressional Democrats, at 17 percent and 19 percent, respectively. The poll of 574 likely Democratic primary voters has a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A Harvard/Harris poll released in April showed Harris with support from 50 percent of Democrats in the primary race, up from 41 percent in March and 39 percent in January and February. Newsom followed Harris with 22 percent support, while Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro received 9 percent. Ocasio-Cortez received 8 percent. Five percent said they would vote for someone else. The poll surveyed 2,745 registered voters from April 23 to April 26 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.87 percentage points. Prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket both list her as the favorite for the 2028 Democratic nomination as of Thursday evening, putting her odds at 17 percent and 20 percent, respectively. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: Ocasio-Cortez renewed her DSA membership as speculation grows about her political future and a possible 2028 presidential run.
news.author: Mandy Taheri
