news.title: How Zohran Mamdani mastered Trump's 'Art of the Deal'
news.text: Every generation has technological habits that confuse the next. Recording TV shows on a thing called a VCR. Sending free SMSes from a bootleg site. Burning CDs. Downloading wallpapers on Santa Banta. Each chore sounds arcanely archaic to the next generation.And the chances are that if you grew up in the early noughties and developed a taste for English music to fit in with anglicised Macaulayputras, you downloaded songs from illegal torrent sites before playing them on Winamp. You might have sung along to how it no longer matters, tried to memorise the lyrics to Lose Yourself (What comes after “Mom’s spaghetti”?) and definitely knew that space may be the final frontier, but it’s made in a Hollywood basement. And much like that, Zohran Mamdani feels like he was conceived in a left-liberal lab to tick all the boxes.The New York mayor is a gallimaufry of values global progressives hold dear: being anti-Israel, being anti-Hindu, being anti-rich, underperforming in SAT exams, trying to pass oneself off as a different race and blaming one’s problems on everyone but oneself.But Mamdani has managed something that none of his progressive peers has: winning while paying the mildest obeisance to the values that his various constituencies hold dear. And he does it while complaining about things without giving the impression of being bitter.Of course, he’s aided and abetted by a mainstream press that waxes lyrical about him as though he’s the second coming of Obama and never gets pushback about his mendacities. For example, during a debate between New York mayoral hopefuls, he claimed that Muslims don’t even exist in Gujarat, an obvious mendacity that would have been called out if it had come from a white politician wearing a red cap. But then again, Kamala Harris has claimed that her grandfather was an Indian freedom fighter, despite his having been part of the Imperial Civil Service under the Crown, and not one American publication has fact-checked her. Those checks are reserved only for Tucker Carlson and white people wearing red caps.But Zohran is exceptionally good at what critics call virtue-signalling but smart people know is making the right noise. Take his smart and masterful handling of the RSS chief’s upcoming event at Madison Square Garden, where he made his mild disdain known before pointing out that it was a private event and he couldn’t do anything to stop it. It was the kind of political manoeuvring that has seen him become the only Democrat who has been able to get more than a fair shake out of Donald Trump.The RSS manoeuvre contained Mamdani’s method in miniature. He gave his progressive supporters the condemnation they wanted, acknowledged that the organisers had the right to hold a private event and ensured that City Hall would not be held responsible for stopping something it had no power to stop. Everyone received something from the deal, especially Mamdani.Interestingly, Donald Trump laid down 11 rules for successful deal-making in The Art of the Deal. Mamdani’s first eight months as mayor suggest that he has followed Trump’s rules more faithfully than most people who actually work for Trump.Rule 1: Think bigMamdani’s campaign was full of big promises to turn the Big Apple into a utopia of affordable homes, parks, schools and union jobs. The minor hitch is that it needs money from a federal government headed by a man he labelled a “despot” and “fascist”. That didn’t stop Mamdani from smiling into Trump’s embrace with a fake New York Daily News header and the promise of something Trump had coveted long before he became POTUS: love from New York. The money might or might not arrive, but Mamdani did get Trump to release an ICE detainee, which shows that he has completely understood Trump’s maxim of thinking big.Rule 2: Protect the downside and the upside will take care of itselfThis is easier said than done, but Mamdani managed it by retaining NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch, who also happens to be a billionaire heiress. This allowed him to distance himself from the politically charged “Defund the Police” chant and even claim credit for major crime and murder rates falling by 5.8% and 24.7% in the first six months of 2026. Mamdani did the same with the Israel Day Parade, appearing with Tisch to announce security for it while staying away, so Palestinians got the boycott they wanted while Jewish New Yorkers received the protection. The art of being present yet absent would have made Schrödinger smile.Rule 3: Maximise your optionsIn Game of Thrones, Cersei Lannister explained to Littlefinger: “Power is power.” And it’s something Mamdani has learnt well. He opposed mayoral control of New York’s public schools but, hours after taking office, reversed course, asked Albany to extend mayoral control and appointed his chancellor.Mamdani promised to use the system more democratically than his predecessors because ending it might have satisfied his progressive supporters but would have surrendered a powerful lever. Instead, he explained to parents that he was in charge.Rule 4: Know your marketNew Yorkers are, perhaps after Indians, the most politically disagreeable people on a vast number of topics, from Gaza and policing to whether Colin Jost should be dropped from SNL, but they all agree that rent is too high. Whatever happens in other parts of the world is secondary.In June, the Rent Guidelines Board, dominated by Mamdani appointees, voted 7-1 to freeze rents on one-year and two-year leases covering roughly one million rent-stabilised apartments. Now, landlords warn that this will lead to wear and tear, reduce maintenance and make the situation worse, but tenants vastly outnumber landlords and, in a democracy, populism, not economic logic, always wins.Rule 5: Use your leverageEvery politician knows that you can’t always get what you want, but if you try hard enough, you will get what you need. Mamdani demanded $5.5 billion from Albany through higher taxes on corporations, warning that failure could force a 9.5% property-tax hike in New York. Governor Kathy Hochul refused but eventually gave enough fiscal help for Mamdani to withdraw the threat, allowing both to declare victory. Many years ago, American scholar Stephen P. Cohen said that Pakistan negotiates with the world by holding a gun to its own head, and while Mamdani might have descended from this side of the border, he showed that you can use leverage with a hint of self-sabotage.Rule 6: Enhance your locationTrump argued that “location, location, location” was misunderstood. A real-estate developer didn’t need the best address, only the best deal, and that could be done with promotion and psychology. He often cited Trump Plaza on Third Avenue as an example.Mamdani appears to have used that logic for municipal groceries, and instead of paying New York’s astronomical rents, the city will place five stores in publicly owned properties, with the city covering rent and property taxes. Unfair to existing grocers? Sure, but that’s how one changes the game and gives the appearance of change without making a real change.Rule 7: Get the word outLong before the attention economy came around, Donald Trump wrote that the greatest product in the world is worthless if nobody knows about it. A tree falling in a forest with no observer makes no noise. That’s one piece of advice that took Mamdani from a virtual unknown to being dubbed the “Everywhere Mayor” by The New Yorker.He appears on reels, streets and Taxi TV, while his Office of Mass Engagement carries his campaign machinery into City Hall. Budgets become explainers, potholes become videos and municipal announcements become content. Most mayors govern and then publicise. Mamdani governs through publicity, ensuring New Yorkers encounter him even when they are trying to hail a cab.Rule 8: Fight backRule 8 is perhaps the one rule that Trump has mastered himself, after facing the full onslaught of America’s four estates for four years before making a comeback to the White House. Mamdani has found his opponent in Amazon, an organisation that makes LuthorCorp look like a mum-and-pop store, through the Delivery Protection Act. This would impose employment and safety rules on warehouses and give Mamdani the pantomime Lex Luthor he needs to keep his base happy.Rule 9: Deliver the goodsNow, this one is open to interpretation as America carries on its never-ending war on Iran under Trump, who appears to have interpreted “goods” as bombs and never-ending ceasefire agreements. Mamdani has opted for parcels. In his first 100 days, the administration secured $9.3 million in restitution for workers, including settlements that produced $5 million for delivery workers. The buses aren’t free and the groceries might not work, but Mamdani has delivered enough “goods” to keep New Yorkers from asking when the rest of the order will arrive.Rule 10: Contain the costsNow, this isn’t a precept the Trump administration follows anymore, given its vacillating trade wars and tariffs. Mamdani, however, discovered fiscal conservatism when the City Council approved one-time payments of up to $10,000 for school paraprofessionals at a cost exceeding $300 million.Despite campaigning with the teachers’ union and promising better pay, Mamdani allowed the measure to become law without signing it and then sued to block it, arguing that it had bypassed collective bargaining.Ergo, a socialist mayor is fighting a union-backed payment to low-paid workers in defence of collective bargaining. Otto von Bismarck would have heartily approved because politics is, after all, the art of the possible.Rule 11: Have funFinally, Mamdani has definitely followed the last rule of Trump’s playbook by looking like the only progressive having fun in the era of Trump. While his reels and social-media game have always been top-drawer, even his teams are performing miracles. Mamdani is now basking in the afterglow of what The Athletic has named “Mamdani’s Sports Summer”, much to the chagrin of Fox acolytes, who are fuming about the Mamdani Effect. But sports fandom runs on superstitions, and Mamdani’s ascent has seen Arsenal win the league for the first time since 2004 and the Knicks win the NBA championship for the first time since 1973.As the Bengali poet MD Ahnaf Hossain, whose art is now being compared to Rabindranath Tagore and Kazi Nazrul Islam, chanted: “My mayor’s Muslim, my bagel’s Jewish, the Pope’s on our side, Knicks in five.”Trump might have written The Art of the Deal, but at this moment, it looks as though it is Zohran Mamdani who is living up to it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
news.summary: Interestingly, Donald Trump laid down 11 rules for successful deal-making inThe Art of the Deal. Mamdani’s first eight months as mayor suggest that he has followed Trump’s rules more faithfully than most people who actually work for Trump.
news.author: Nirmalya Dutta

news.title: JD Vance's Chances of Beating Trump Jr., Rubio in New 2028 Poll
news.text: Vice President JD Vance leads a hypothetical 2028 Republican presidential primary with 32 percent, ahead of Donald Trump Jr. at 19 percent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 12 percent. The McLaughlin & Associates findings offer an early look at the competition to inherit President Donald Trump’s political coalition, even though the next presidential election remains more than two years away. Republican voters have not settled on a successor, but Vance starts with the widest support across the party’s principal demographic and ideological groups, according to this latest poll. Key Points Why It Matters No candidate has formally entered the 2028 contest, yet early polling can reveal which politicians begin with durable name recognition and an identifiable partisan base. Vance benefits from serving as vice president, while Trump Jr.’s latest improvement suggests that the contest for voters most closely aligned with the president is not settled. Vance Leads as Trump Jr. Gains Ground McLaughlin & Associates surveyed 1,000 likely general-election voters nationally from August 18 to 24. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points at the 95 percent confidence level, with the Republican primary question based on 433 respondents. Vance’s 32 percent is below his series high of 43 percent in April 2025. His support has otherwise remained mostly in the 30s since March of that year, suggesting a substantial starting constituency but no commanding majority. Trump Jr. has recovered from 12 percent in May 2026 to 19 percent in August. He was as high as 26 percent in December 2025, when he came within eight points of Vance. Rubio’s latest decline interrupts a longer rise. After polling mainly in low single digits through 2025, he reached 10 percent in March 2026 and peaked at 15 percent between May and July. How Vance’s Coalition Breaks Down Vance receives 38 percent among conservatives, compared with 25 percent among moderates and 11 percent among liberals in the Republican sample. He also takes 35 percent among respondents who voted for Trump in 2024. His support is balanced by sex, standing at 32 percent among men and 33 percent among women. Age creates a wider divide: 38 percent of voters over 55 choose him, against 27 percent of those under 55. Trump Jr. also performs better among older voters, drawing 25 percent from the over-55 group and 12 percent from younger respondents. Rubio shows the reverse pattern, taking 19 percent among voters under 55 and 6 percent among those above that age. What The Potential Candidates Have Said Vance has left the door open without committing. In June, he said he and Trump would discuss his future after the 2026 midterms, adding that he did not want consideration of another job to make him a worse vice president. "I have no doubt that the president of the United States is going to be very supportive of anything that I ultimately decide to do," Vance told CBS Sunday Morning. "But we really just haven't talked about what that thing will be." Neither Vance nor Rubio has announced a 2028 campaign. Speaking about his relationship with the secretary of state, Vance said both were focused on the administration’s current work rather than positioning themselves for office years in advance. Their public appearances have emphasized cooperation, with Rubio calling Vance a friend during a February State Department event. Trump Jr. denied considering a bid after a 2025 report said he was weighing one, calling the claims “bulls***” and pointing to his support for Vance’s selection as his father’s running mate. Democrats Face Their Own Unsettled Field Former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 29 percent leaves her 13 points ahead of California Governor Gavin Newsom, but below the 35 percent she recorded in December 2024. Newsom has also retreated from his series high of 22 percent in September and October 2025. A separate Emerson College poll tested hypothetical general-election contests rather than Democratic primary preferences. Pete Buttigieg led both Vance and Rubio by 5 points, while Harris led Vance by 4 points but trailed Rubio by 5. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and Newsom led Rubio by 3 and 2 points, respectively. Emerson surveyed 1,000 likely voters on August 16 and 17, 2026, with a plus or minus 3 percentage point margin of error. What Happens Next For Republicans, the immediate question is whether Trump Jr. can sustain his recent recovery. Vance remains the clear leader, but the poll describes an opening position rather than a reliable forecast of the 2028 nomination. For Democrats, the question is whether Harris can hold her lead as the prospective field takes shape. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Trump Jr. posts a three-point gain among likely Republican voters, while Kamala Harris holds a 13-point advantage among Democrats.
news.author: Sam Stevenson

news.title: What Did Socialist Amish Shah Bail on Last Night's Debate?
news.text:
Amish Shah is a radical socialist running for Congress in Arizona's 1st District. He's got ties to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), backed Bernie Sanders for president at a DSA event in 2019, and loves AOC.

He ran for Congress in 2024 and underperformed both Ruben Gallego and Kamala Harris, but that hasn't stopped him from trying again to get back into Congress to enact his far-left socialist agenda. That includes raising taxes on Arizona families by $4,000 a year, giving sanctuary to illegal aliens, and defunding the police.

Perhaps that's why Shah ducked out on yesterday's debate with Jay Feely.

And Shah was nowhere to be found.

"As for the Democratic candidate, Amish Shah, he declined our invitation to participate in tonight's discussion," said host Ted Simons.

Feely called Shah's absence "disappointing."

He's hoping you never learn who he really is. https://t.co/pQkXYL1Ffq— Jay Feely (@jayfeely) August 27, 2026

"Shah knows his socialist views & support for Bernie Sanders are deeply unpopular. He's hoping you never learn who he really is," he wrote on X.

When there is an opportunity to explain what he would do for his district, Socialist Shah is no where to he found. "Instead, Jay Feely actually showed up to the debate, like he will do in Congress for the people of the 1st district. If we can trust Amish Shah to show up in a debate, how can we trust him to represent the people of Arizona?" Flores Stan wrote.

This is correct. If Shah can't be bothered to show up to a debate and answer tough questions, what will he do for Arizona voters? We know some of it — higher taxes, defunded police, sanctuary policies — and maybe that explains why Shah refused to answer questions.

news.title: MS NOW Pleads Democrats To Stop 'Infighting About Random Streamers'
news.text:
The only reason why The Bulwark podcaster Tim Miller is an MS NOW analyst is because he and his Bulwark colleagues have portrayed themselves as the epitome of moral virtue for leaving the Republican Party in the aftermath of the political rise of Donald Trump. However, on Wednesday’s edition of The Moment with Katy Tur, Miller pleaded with Democrats to stop “infighting about random streamers,” by which he meant anti-Semitic 9/11 apologist and Mao fan, Hasan Piker.

Tur began by asking, “Tim, do you think Democrats are reaching out effectively, or are they battling their own demons?”

Miller began his response by stating, “I think it's a mixed bag. I think the one thing that Democrats are doing good is they're talking about affordability. I think some Democrats think that, like, saying the word “affordability” is like an amulet that allows them to kind of check the box. And I think that they're going to have to go a little bit further than that. You know, and I think that there's some who are doing that really well. Like we've mentioned, Talarico. I think even the center-left Democrats could learn a lot from Zohran. Like he doesn't talk about affordability, like it's an academic exercise. If you listen to his speeches and his content, he's usually giving, like, tangible examples of… people, you know, who are struggling and what he's going to do to help them.”

The Bulwark's Tim Miller thinks Democrats shouldn't reckon with Hasan Piker, "less infighting about random streamers as well" and "[El-Sayed's] got to also convince the kind of Bernie to Trump voters, like these are the types of people that he needs to win over to get over the… pic.twitter.com/VxHNKbCMOH— Alex Christy (@alexchristy17) August 27, 2026

He then added, “I think the Democrats could do a little bit better on that… less infighting about random streamers as well. So, you know, there's a little room for growth, but they're doing pretty good.”

Piker is not just a random streamer. He is someone both El-Sayed and the media have tried to normalize. In El-Sayed’s case that meant campaigning with him and refusing to denounce him. In the media’s case it meant platforming him and giving him glowing profiles. Now that he has become politically toxic, they are now pretending they want nothing to do with him.

As it was, Tur wondered, “What does that mean?”

Miller responded that El-Sayed has to win over the “Bernie-to-Trump voters,” but that Democrats aren’t helping themselves, “I think that there's a lot of fighting back and forth between him and, like, this Michigan Congresswoman Hilary Scholten and others, you know, about whether he's too close to Hasan Piker or whether he's not distancing himself enough. And they're fighting back and forth. And, you know, he was on Jesse Watters this week, kind of like arguing about, you know, trans youth gender reassignment surgery. I'm not sure how helpful that is. So, you know, there can be a little bit of a—more of an eye on the ball in some of these races.”

For Miller, Trump was a bridge too far, but Piker is just a minor irritant that Democrats need to ignore to win back power. Unfortunately for him, that is not how politics works. El-Sayed and Michigan Democrats made their bed, and now they will have to lie in it.

news.title: Democrats try to brush aside Woke 1
news.text:
As a possible national candidate, Ocasio-Cortez obviously has a motive to brush aside, as she did with a charmingly self-deprecatory laugh, the exotic positions she and other Democrats took on issues, particularly after the death of George Floyd in May 2020 and the ensuing multicity violent rioting.

They included demands to “defund the police” or even abolish police departments, to step up the already institutionalized demands for “diversity, equity, and inclusion” hiring and promotions in bureaucracies, public and private, for racial reparations. These weren’t just words: Cities such as New York, San Francisco, Chicago, and Minneapolis did hustle to partially defund their police departments. 

The Floyd riots and calls for defunding police were immediately followed by a sharp spike upward in violent crime. Liberals have characterized that spike as a response to COVID-19, but charts compiled by writer Steve Sailer make it clear that the spike began not with the lockdowns but with the riots and Woke 1 depolicing. 

At the same time, the lockdowns, enforced with Woke 1 censoriousness, were causing not just economic damage but also long-lasting harm to children who were kept out of teacher union-run schools long after it was clear children were not vectors of the virus. And Woke 1 transgender demands, for biological men on women’s sports teams and public financing of even pre-adults’ gender transition surgery, were advanced by the Biden administration and endorsed by Harris.

The political damage was clear, and probably noticed by the increasingly politically adept Ocasio-Cortez, who put out by far the most effective single ad in the 2024 campaign, saying that “Kamala Harris is for they/them and Donald Trump is for you.” 

Now there are numerous signs that the nation is putting Woke 1 so far in the rearview mirror as to be invisible and has little appetite for Woke 2. Items include:

(1) The lack of visible vehement protests at the elimination of DEI programs — racial quotas and preferences — in federal regulations, in many state and local governments, and even in their strongholds in the universities. 

You hear grumbling about the Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, but nothing like the politically charged attacks on its 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade. There’s covert opposition and attempts to retain DEI under different labels, but you don’t hear Democratic candidates talking about the issue.

(2) Similarly, there’s a dog-who-didn’t-bark response to the Trump administration’s effective shutdown of illegal immigration on the southern border. Missing from the political dialogue have been media stories about the asylum-seekers who are obliged now to pursue their claims not from somewhere in the continental United States but from a not particularly helpful or sympathetic Mexico or somewhere even more distant. 

(3) Violent crime rates seem sharply down. After the Floyd riots, homicides rose even more in 2021 and seemed on a trajectory to reverse all the enormous progress in crime reduction accomplished since the reforms pioneered by Rudy Giuliani in New York in the 1990s. Homicides declined in 2025 to below the lowest numbers of the post-Giuliani years, and the FBI reported that violent crime dropped 9.3%, the biggest drop since 1936.

For 2026, statistics aren’t fully available, but starkly lower rates of violent crime in New York and a huge 2020s drop in homicides in Baltimore. 

Why the huge drop in violent crime? No one is sure, but it comes as Democratic politicians are hastening to assure us that they never actually really wanted to abolish the police and the prisons when they were saying so back in Woke 1.

(4) The revelations of the hypocrisy and lies of Dr. Anthony Fauci and other public health officials during the COVID-19 epidemic. Fauci, who delighted in partying with Washington elites, according to his diaries, had to sit mute and invoke the Fifth Amendment as he was attacked credibly for having misled the public. Masking, he admitted privately, didn’t prevent disease spread, even while he urged penalties for non-maskers. The vaccine, while reducing deaths, did not prevent transmission, as he had assured the nation.

Fauci’s efforts to discredit as “a conspiracy theory” the argument that the virus spread from a leak from the Wuhan laboratory he financed increasingly look very much like an effort to cover up the evidence that he financed the lab’s gain-of-function research surreptitiously (to make the virus more dangerous) in violation of a presidential order. The initial order, by the way, came from President Barack Obama, not President Donald Trump. 

Against this evidence of the discrediting of Woke 1 come recent victories and near victories of members of or sympathizers with the Democratic Socialists of America, whose platform calls for the abolition of police and prisons. Those candidates have been emphasizing economic issues, however, which pass muster in Democratic primaries but may not in general electorates in states such as Michigan. 

What is not apparent in the political landscape is nostalgia for Woke 1 police defunding, for heavy-handed statism like Fauci’s COVID-19 regime, or for a revival of the Biden administration’s open borders immigration policy. Democrats may be able to capitalize on the current Trump slump this year. But for 2028, they may not be able to dismiss questions about Woke 1 —and Woke 2 — as flippantly as AOC tried to do this August.

news.title: Dolly Parton blazed a path that modern country stars can’t follow
news.text:
Dolly Parton made a lot of things across her 60-plus-year career: massive hit songs, a theme park, a children’s literacy initiative that gave away over 300 million books, movies of both the smash-hit and cult classic variety. But she shied away from making political statements. 

This might seem like an odd thing to say about a country star whose coiffed blonde wig inched close to the heavenly host up until her death on Monday at 80, a down-home diva whose songs made her identifiable by just a mononym, whose blindingly bedazzled, highly structured outfits made her recognized by just her silhouette. Parton preferred to let her closet make the statements, while quietly building a kind of everybody-love-everybody progressivism that promoted equality and kindness while remaining mostly off-the-record. 

In the public eye, Parton the person was always willing to take a backseat to her persona. She turned the “dumb blonde” assumptions on the audience, crafting a comedic alter ego that happened to share her name. Although it was Dolly Parton taking questions from late-night hosts in countless, breezy interviews, it was “Dolly Parton” answering. Dolly the character wasn’t taken seriously, and that steered interviewers away from asking her about serious topics.

Though she consciously and strenuously attempted to avoid labels like feminist and activist, Parton’s actions occasionally made her inner beliefs undeniable. She was writing songs in support of gay family members back in 1991, the first mainstream country artist to do so. She took a ride on the Magic School Bus in 1996 to stress the importance of recycling and environmental conservation. You can find her on the cover of Out Magazine in 1997, celebrating her legions of LGBTQ fans. Here she comes again, penning a song for the 2005 movie “Transamerica” that would go on to receive an Academy Award nomination. And there you go, trying to make the “love is love” ethos of her public persona into something like a personal politics.

But Parton could be hard to pin down. She’s the centerpiece of “9 to 5,” a movie about unionization and pushing back against workplace sexual harassment. If you somehow missed that star turn — her first — don’t worry; she sings the theme song. Still, she quickly shut down Elizabeth Warren’s presidential campaign in 2019 when they attempted to use “9 to 5” at rallies as a nod to the candidate’s pro-labor activism. Parton repeatedly refused to accept the Presidential Medal of Freedom from both Donald Trump and Joe Biden. Buried somewhere in her reasoning was likely something along these lines: “Dolly Parton” isn’t political, therefore Dolly Parton’s songs cannot be political.

The singer’s extensive philanthropic record mostly pushed the importance of literacy and higher education, a view that has been coded as left-of-center thanks to the actions of Republicans, who have spent several decades fleeing and sometimes sabotaging public education. Parton’s AIDS activism and LGBTQ advocacy puts her well to the left of the average MAGA fan socially. Despite this, she’s universally adored across the political spectrum. A poll released just this April found she had the highest favorability ratings of any American. 

How was this country legend able to walk the line so deftly? Why was she able to work toward progressive goals without facing any backlash from conservative fans? And will any mainstream country star ever be able to avoid getting bogged down in culture war battles the way Dolly did? 

That last question is the easiest and quickest to answer: No. The why is less simple. 

Dolly was able to just be Dolly, in part, because of how long she’d been Dolly. She predated our overheated era of cable-news slapfights as a massive star and national treasure who never took herself too seriously. She was famously in on all the jokes about her. She launched her Imagination Library in the late 1980s, well before a time when a centralized charity sending out books directly to children would be subject to immense scrutiny, outside of fringe cranks on high alert for any whiff of a New World Order. Parton was cemented as an icon before two events turned country music stardom entirely on its head. 

The Sept. 11 attacks and the advent of social media fundamentally changed the shape of country music and what it meant to be a chart-topper. The latter gave rise to the idea that fans had a right to know more about their favorite artists, up to and including where they stood on specific political issues. The former was the genesis of the Global War on Terror, an atrocity that drew a red line through American culture and bluntly asked a question familiar to Parton’s fellow Appalachians: Which side are you on?

In the aftermath of 9/11, country music radio became a font of rah-rah troop support and war-boosterism. As Lee Greenwood’s 1984 hit “God Bless The U.S.A.” returned to the chart, 1990s hitmaker Alan Jackson took a break from tender love songs to write a schmaltzy tribute to the lives lost at Ground Zero, the Pentagon and the field in Pennsylvania. Toby Keith drooled over artillery and warned “we’ll put a boot in your a*s, it’s the American way,” and Darryl Worley wrote propaganda pieces for the war’s expansion. The jingoism soon became all too much for The Chicks, the best-selling country band in recorded history, whose frontwoman Natalie Maines said during a London show kicking off the band’s “Top of the World” tour that she was “ashamed” then-President George W. Bush was from her home state of Texas. “We do not want this war, this violence,” she said, referring to the administration’s imminent plans to invade Iraq. 

The backlash was swift and immediate. Knee-jerk patriots who felt betrayed by these bluegrass traditionalists turned mega-stars crushed their Chicks’ CDs in public protests. They argued that Maines’ criticism, which came on foreign soil, was cowardly. Maines countered that she was responding to current events, but she apologized to the fans who felt hurt — and then she recanted. The Chicks’ songs were blacklisted on many country radio stations, and remained that way for years. While the band never wavered on their criticism of Bush, and even doubled down on it in their 2006 hit “Not Ready to Make Nice,” the message was clear to any acts without the mega-fame of The Chicks: Shut up and sing. 

The resulting two decades of conservative, nostalgic hits on country radio have made Republican leanings cloaked in back-home nostalgia the default pose of country music’s A-list. At the same time, fan pressure to offer unambiguous political statements has grown. 

Parton’s solo career spanned equally divisive times, launching at the height of the Vietnam War and carrying on for everything that came afterwards. But the assumption that she should have a stance on issues of the day was nowhere near as strong then. By the time social media made political heat checks commonplace, Parton was exempt from the demand for answers.

Start your day with essential news from Salon.
Sign up for our free morning newsletter, Crash Course.

Maybe it’s because journalists and fans knew what they would get. In a May 2023 interview with journalist Jacob Saboroff, she was asked about what could well be her most political song. “World on Fire,” she sang, “Greedy politicians present and past / They wouldn’t know the truth if it bit ‘em in the a*s.” Parton told Soboroff she was singing about “All of ‘em. Any of ‘em.” 

“I don’t think any of ‘em are trying hard enough,” she said. “I’m sure we’re all trying, but I just really think often that they worry more about their party than they do about the people. If we just do what we felt was the right thing, rather than who’s going to lose, or who’s going to win this, or who’s going to look better if they do this. None of them are working from the heart.”

At the same time, allegations of GOP sympathies dogged country star turned pop icon Taylor Swift for years before she explicitly endorsed Democratic candidate Kamala Harris for president in 2024. If Zac Brown and Luke Bryan were going to turn the charts into troops salutes and MAGA boat parade soundtracks, then actual veteran Zach Bryan was going to have to go on the record with an anti-ICE track. Although Kacey Musgraves has singles in the Parton school of “let people live,” she doesn’t have the luxury of public neutrality that Dolly did.

Now even Dolly-esque clowning can’t save country music’s current stars from having to take unambiguous positions. In the music video for Musgraves’ recent single “Dry Spell,” she reflects on striking out as a single woman while ogling suggestively shaped produce in the grocery store. On her current tour, she descends to the stage on a pair of mirror-covered testicles, literal disco balls. Still, when she speaks out in support of American immigrants as one of the genre’s most prominent progressives, she’s branded a traitor by conservative country fans. Musgraves’ fanbase wants her to speak up, if only to distance herself from the MAGA-until-proven-otherwise pack, but doing so is risky and messy.

No such backlash came for Dolly when she spoke out against Tennessee’s anti-trans laws or in support of the George Floyd protests. She was able to hold a consistent “play nice” line because of her unassailable career and how long she’d been at it. It’s a stance that wouldn’t be allowed from anyone but Dolly, and one that will now almost certainly never be accepted again. Like her rise from the deepest rural poverty to beloved multi-millionaire, it’s one more yet part of her story that is entirely singular.
news.summary: Parton's outwardly apolitical, quietly radical balancing act can't be repeated in the social media age
news.author: Alex Galbraith

Jelly Roll risks sparking Trump feud as he DEFENDS 'fat pig' jab and says US presidents 'should be able to handle a few jokes'

By ADAM S. LEVY, US SENIOR SHOWBUSINESS REPORTER

Jelly Roll didn't back down after backlash to a joke he made referring to President Donald Trump as a 'fat pig' while serving as guest host of Jimmy Kimmel Live! this week.

On Tuesday, the three-time Grammy winner, 41, addressed the blowback from people who said he was essentially insulting his own audience after taking shots at Trump's weight during his monologue on Monday's episode. 

He said he was surprised that the remarks were 'the weirdest thing I've ever done to stun people,' describing himself as a 'former felon;' 'a drug dealer who has lost 300 pounds;' and a person who has 'tattoos all over his face.'

Jelly Roll, whose full name is Jason Bradley DeFord, added, 'What a turn of events: Who would have guessed I'd get in more trouble with the president than Rosie O'Donnell?'

The Save Me vocalist said he felt that Trump should have thicker skin being in the Oval Office.

Jelly Roll, 41, didn't back down after backlash to a joke he made about President Donald Trump while serving as Jimmy Kimmel Live!'s guest host 

'Let's be honest for a second - any U.S. president should be able to handle a few jokes, right?' Jelly Roll said. 'They should also be able to handle gas prices, healthcare and the occasional international conflict, but beggars can't be choosers.'

The Daily Mail has reached out to representatives for Jelly Roll for further comment on the story.

The country music star raised eyebrows on Monday after directing punchlines in the president's direction when speaking about the IndyCar Freedom 250 event in Washington, D.C.

Jelly Roll joked that 'the president seemed to enjoy the IndyCar race, which was a real switch-up for him because normally he only likes his own race.

'Trump also drove around the track in his motorcade doing what they call the "lap of honor" - which sounds like a loyalty program at a strip club.'

He then shifted the topic to Trump's appearance, saying that the Sunday drive marked 'the only laps Trump's been doing lately.'

After a montage of clips of Trump alluding to people's appearances, Jelly Roll said, 'Well, Mr. President, from one fat pig to another, take it from me that physical fitness is very important.

'It’s crazy, think about this, y’all. In the last few years, I’ve lost 300 pounds. That means I’ve lost an entire Donald Trump - and let’s be honest, based on his approval ratings, it seems like most of the country wants to do the same thing.'

Jelly Roll on Tuesday said that in the wake of the controversial monologue, he faced pushback from some folks online since he 'didn't treat the president with reverence and dignity.'

'They see a guy that looks like me and assume the only opinion I have is whether I prefer my meth crystal or classic!'

Jelly Roll said jokes about the president come with the territory of the high-profile position, noting the Democrat who Trump prevailed over in the 2024 presidential election.

news.title: The Latest Marquette Poll Is Bad News for David Crowley. Here's Why.
news.text:
Yesterday, the Marquette University (MU) Law poll dropped, showing that Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany are in a dead heat in the Wisconsin governor's race, with 12 percent of registered voters remaining undecided.

The governor’s race is tied among all registered voters at 44% each for Crowley and Tiffany, with 12% undecided. #mulawpoll— MULawPoll (@MULawPoll) August 26, 2026

Among likely voters, Crowley only has a five point lead.

A new Marquette Law School Poll of Wisconsin finds that in the race for governor, Democrat David Crowley is leading Republican Tom Tiffany among likely voters by 49% to 44%, with 7% undecided. #mulawpoll— MULawPoll (@MULawPoll) August 26, 2026

This is good news for Tom Tiffany, and here's why: the August MU Law poll has always overestimated the Democrat.

Today’s Marquette University Law School Poll is setting the narrative that David Crowley has a comfortable lead, but I crunched the data and found that Marquette’s August poll always dramatically overestimates Democrat support. https://t.co/u0sYGHDq6w— Dan O'Donnell (@DanODonnellShow) August 26, 2026

Here's more:

Since its inception, Marquette’s August poll has not just been wildly unsuccessful at predicting the ultimate result of a November race; it has also overestimated Democrats’ support by an average of 3.5%. Even when taking out the anomalous 2016 presidential election (when every poll right up until Election Day) was enormously wrong, the average overestimation of Democrat support by 2.1%.Just once did it get a race exactly right in August—its 2024 presidential election poll showing President Trump beating Kamala Harris by a point—and in five of the nine August polls of presidential and gubernatorial races it has conducted over the past decade, it has been off by six or more points. In every single one of those five massive misses, it dramatically overestimated the support of the Democrat.Just once, in that August 2024 presidential poll, did it ever show the Republican candidate leading even though Republican candidates went on to win their respective races four times in nine elections.Just three times in nine polls did the August Marquette poll overestimate Republican support: In 2018, when it showed incumbent governor Scott Walker and challenger Tony Evers tied (Evers went on to win the race by a point) and incumbent Senator Tammy Baldwin up three on challenger Leah Vukmir (Baldwin won by 11), and in 2022, when it had Evers leading Republican Tim Michels by two points (Evers won by three).

O'Donnell theorizes the attacks on Crowley's data center stance are damaging his campaign.

Proof that "Data Center David" is doing real damage to Crowley. Over the ten-year history of this poll, Democrats usually lead by 5-10 in August. https://t.co/HifwJPuhXr— Dan O'Donnell (@DanODonnellShow) August 26, 2026

And here's more behind that.

Proof that "Data Center David" is doing real damage to Crowley. Over the ten-year history of this poll, Democrats usually lead by 5-10 in August. https://t.co/HifwJPuhXr— Dan O'Donnell (@DanODonnellShow) August 26, 2026

"Data centers are now the issue in the governor's race and Republican Tom Tiffany has staked out the position that the overwhelming majority of Wisconsin is on, and David Crowley's past comments pretty much throughout the primary are positioning him as the guy who wants to bring more data centers to communities that aren't his. And that's the critical thing," O'Donnell said.

"Crowley is from Milwaukee and the rest of Wisconsin always views Milwaukee, rightly or wrongly, with a good bit of suspicion," he continued. "Yes, it's the economic engine of the entire state, but it's also seen as forcing its will on the other 71 counties. The Milwaukee County Executive very publicly earlier this month saying that he wants to 'share the wealth of data' centers with the rest of the state' now that Milwaukee, Madison, and Green Bay already have them, is being interpreted as meaning, 'Yeah, no, my community of Milwaukee and my favored liberal cities of Madison and Green Bay don't want or need data centers. But you smaller, Republican, rural, and exurban communities? You need them so that you can be the economic engine of the state in the economy of tomorrow, absorbing all of the negatives of data centers while we in Milwaukee, Madison, and Green Bay generate the revenue in the form of state tax income, while absorbing none of the negatives."

"That is a big, big problem."

This writer has lived in Milwaukee County her entire life, and the rest of the state does not like the county much. As O'Donnell said, many see Milwaukee as sucking up the state's tax dollars while not addressing the crime and poverty that are rampant in the city of Milwaukee, crime that also spills out into the suburbs in nearby counties.

And given Crowley's mismanagement of the County — from high taxes to budget deficits to crime — he's got an uphill battle going into November.

news.title: Jelly Roll sends message to MAGA fans as Trump 'fat pig' jab sparks backlash
news.text:
Jelly Roll has stood by a jab at Donald Trump on Jimmy Kimmel Live! in which he called the US president a 'fat pig'.

The grammy-winning musician had been guest hosting on the show, and didn't hold back in his criticism of Trump.

Addressing the president directly, he said: "Well, Mr. President, from one fat pig to another, take it from me that physical fitness is very important."

Jelly Roll then went on to talk about his own weight loss journey, before making a barbed remark at Trump's approval ratings.

"It’s crazy, think about this, y’all," he said. "In the last few years, I’ve lost 300 pounds. That means I’ve lost an entire Donald Trump - and let’s be honest, based on his approval ratings, it seems like most of the country wants to do the same thing."

The barbs at Trump's physical fitness came after a section on the IndyCar Freedom 250 event which was held in Washington D.C, with Jelly Roll saying: "The president seemed to enjoy the IndyCar race, which was a real switch-up for him because normally he only likes his own race."

He went on to describe Trump's motorcade driving round the track in a 'lap of honor', quipping that it 'sounds like a loyalty program at a strip club', and that this is 'the only laps Trump's been doing lately.'

The jokes have of course resulted in a widespread backlash against the musician over his jokes about Trump, with Jelly Roll remarking: "What a turn of events: Who would have guessed I'd get in more trouble with the president than Rosie O'Donnell?"

Jelly Roll, whose real name is Jason Bradley DeFord, went on to stick by the jokes, saying: "Let's be honest for a second - any US president should be able to handle a few jokes, right?"

He added: "They should also be able to handle gas prices, healthcare and the occasional international conflict, but beggars can't be choosers."

The musician had also said that a lot of people who watched the show may have been 'surprised that I had any opinions at all.'

"They see a guy that looks like me and assume the only opinion I have is whether I prefer my meth crystal or classic!" he said.

There were also people who shared their disapproval of Jelly Roll making jokes about Trump in this way, but the musician had a very clear message for them.

"Look, y'all, I get it there's some people are mad at me for goofing on Trump. But if you wanted me to make jokes about Kamala Harris, you should have voted for her!" he said.

Some of those accused Jelly Roll of not treating the president with 'with reverence and dignity', to which he quipped: "I want to remind y'all that I go by the name Jelly Roll - I don't even treat myself with reverence and dignity!"

He added: "So for those who threaten to stop listening to my music based on my comments last night, I just want to say with conviction - go right ahead - cause I'm gonna keep speaking my truth, or my name isn't Post Malone!"
news.summary: The musician appeared as a guest host on Jimmy Kimmel Live! where he made a big jab at the US president
news.author: Kit Roberts

news.title: US Education Department Appears to Positively Compare Trump to Hitler in Now-Deleted Promo Video
news.text: The US Department of Education deleted a promotional video after critics pointed out that its attempt to praise Donald Trump appeared to liken him to Adolf Hitler.The department's official X account shared the video Wednesday, using a scene from Darkest Hour, the 2017 film about former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill. In the clip, Churchill, played by Gary Oldman, shouts: 'You cannot reason with a tiger when your head is in its mouth.'The video then cuts to a montage of Trump clips, apparently presenting the line as a dramatic endorsement of the president's confrontational style. The Department of Education captioned the post: 'No one does it like us,' followed by a tiger emoji.But viewers quickly noticed the problem. In the film, the 'tiger' Churchill is referring to is Adolf Hitler, as he rejects the idea that Britain should negotiate with Nazi Germany.Critics Say Department Missed the PointThe post was quickly mocked across X, with users asking whether the department understood the scene it had used. Matt Rein, a Democratic National Committee official, wrote: 'the 'tiger' being referenced here is Hitler btw.'Another user put it more bluntly: 'Our tax dollars are paying for the department of education to make videos comparing hitler to trump. Thats a thing now. That happened.'The X account Headquarters, which was previously associated with Kamala Harris' presidential campaign, also criticised the post.'They fired the employees who help fund teachers and students but kept the taxpayer-funded fancam editor,' the account wrote.Another user said: 'Aside from the fact that this video nakedly compares Trump to Adolf Hitler what does it have to do with education?'Community Note Flags Hitler ReferenceThe post eventually received a Community Note on X, which linked to a longer version of the Darkest Hour scene and explained the context of Churchill's line. The note pointed out that the 'tiger' in question was Hitler, not a general symbol of toughness or victory.The Department of Education deleted the post shortly afterwards. The agency has not publicly explained how the video was approved or whether anyone involved in its social media operation understood the film reference.Latest Trump Meme ControversyThe deleted promo is the latest example of official or Trump-linked social media posts drawing outrage for strange or inflammatory imagery. In recent months, Trump has faced criticism for sharing AI-generated posts and memes targeting political opponents or placing himself in religious and historical imagery.Earlier this year, he faced backlash after sharing a racist video depicting Barack Obama and Michelle Obama as apes. The clip was later deleted, though Trump did not apologise.In another controversy, Trump posted an image portraying himself as Jesus Christ during a public feud with Pope Leo XIV. He deleted that post after criticism from religious groups and some Republicans, then later shared another image showing himself embraced by Jesus in front of an American flag.A Self-Own From an Education AgencyThe Department of Education's video stood out because it was posted by an agency responsible for schools and learning, making the mistake even more embarrassing.'The department of education being so profoundly illiterate as to not know what this scene is referring to is just beautifully poetic,' one user wrote.The post may have been intended to present Trump as bold and uncompromising. Instead, it handed critics an easy attack line: a taxpayer-funded promo that accidentally made the exact comparison the White House would presumably want to avoid.
news.author: Terence Repelente

news.title: Why cattle ranchers are fuming at Trump
news.text:

news.title: Iran war anniversary: Risks rise for Republicans heading into midterms
news.text:
BETHLEHEM, Pa. (AP) — Mike Gibbons sat out the presidential election two years ago, frustrated that Democrat Kamala Harris did not take a stronger stand against Israel’s war in Gaza and unable to bring himself to cast a vote for Republican Donald Trump.

That is not his plan this year. 

The 33-year-old restaurant server in this eastern Pennsylvania town that once housed one of the world’s largest steelmakers is eager to vote for any Democrat he can in November. As the war with Iran that Trump initially said would last weeks surpasses six months on Friday, Gibbons is feeling the fallout every time he fills his tank at nearly $1 per gallon more than last year. 

“The price of gas affects the price of everything and the price of everything’s up and my pay hasn’t gone up,” he said. “I’m doing blue no matter who this time.”

The Iran war has reshaped the rapidly approaching midterm elections, undermining Trump’s campaign pledge to steer clear of foreign conflicts and challenging Republicans who would rather focus on their tax cuts as they cling to narrow majorities in Congress. 

While the president’s supporters are undeterred, the war’s unpopularity and economic ripple effects could tilt the scales in tightly contested U.S. House districts like the one in Bethlehem, where Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie is one of this year’s most vulnerable incumbents. 

Midterm elections are always difficult for the party in power in Washington. But interviews with voters around the country show how a war that Trump expected to end with a swift victory could undermine the final years of his presidency.

Many US adults say the war has not been worth fighting

About two-thirds of U.S. adults say the war with Iran has not been worth fighting, according to a July poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. That includes the vast majority of Democrats and independents, as well as more than one-third of Republicans.

Although Trump has long criticized Iran’s leadership, he did little to prepare Americans or allies for such a lengthy conflict. Republican President George W. Bush, for instance, spent more than a year making a case for launching a war in Iraq through speeches and attempts to build an international coalition. Trump did none of that.

Trump has refused to acknowledge the war’s cost, saying this month he would “never apologize” for higher prices stemming from it and insisting he did “the right thing” to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. His administration announced new sanctions this week in an attempt to further isolate Tehran. 

In Congress, Republicans have shifted from initially cheerleading Trump’s moves in Iran to expressing concern about the toll of the war. But the party has largely unified to block measures that would curb Trump’s war powers and leaders have shown no interest in cutting off money for the war, preferring to portray Democrats as extremists who cannot be trusted to govern.

Democrats who were blamed just two years ago for presiding over high prices see an opportunity to turn the issue back on their opponents. As part of his comeback U.S. Senate bid in Ohio, Sherrod Brown released an ad this week filmed at a gas station as he said “the cost of gas is out of control and we’re the ones paying for it.”

Speaking to a group of older adults recently in a Republican-dominated swath of western Maryland, Democratic U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks blamed higher prices on the war. Heading into November, she encouraged fellow Democrats to stay focused on the war’s impact and what it says about Trump’s leadership.

“We ought to be saying what is obvious, which is our country is heading in the wrong direction,” she said in an interview.

That resonates with voters such as Brandon Bane, a fast-food worker in Bakersfield, California, where Republican Rep. David Valadao is also in a competitive congressional race. Bane, who described himself as a political independent, said he often has to balance paying rent and groceries, noting high gas prices have only added to the challenge.

“It hasn’t been worth it at all,” he said of the war, adding that he plans to vote for Valadao’s challenger, Democrat Randy Villegas. 

Melissa Wegman, a Democratic retiree who is also from Bakersfield, said she was shocked when the pump recently whirled to $128 to fill the tank on her SUV. 

“I have to manage a budget,” she said.

Some voters are sticking with Republicans 

But there is a risk, too, that the war does not provide Democrats with the political boost they are expecting. 

While there is plenty of frustration about prices, there are also voters willing to make adjustments without blaming Republicans. Many remain aligned with Trump and are not interested in seeing Democrats return to power. 

North Carolina is a top pickup opportunity for Democrats hoping to flip a U.S. Senate seat. But at the State Farmers Market in Raleigh, North Carolina, Lucienda Lowe of Sugarloaf Orchards said her faith in Trump is solid. 

“There has to be a reason why they’re over there,” she said. “They wouldn’t be over there doing that if there wasn’t something more going on than what we’re seeing.”

She has not raised her prices on apples even as fuel and fertilizer costs soar. Her family has been farming since 1846 so she feels resilient to weather the next rough patch and tells others to do the same. 

“Suck it up, buttercup,” she said.

Similarly in Iowa, where Democrats are bullish on their prospects of flipping everything from a U.S. Senate seat and the governor’s mansion to several U.S. House races, Larry Cole said higher gas prices as a result of the war are just the “nature of the beast.”

The 66-year-old Republican service manager from Perry, Iowa, said he will back Republicans in this midterm elections and does not want to see Democrats gain control in either chamber. He said Trump has taken action that other presidents were not willing to do to keep Iran in check.

Trump “hit them where they need to be hit,” Cole said.

Mark Duffy, 65, of Scottsdale, Arizona, said he did not expect the Iran war to go on as long as it has, but it has not had material effects on his life.

“I didn’t think it would go this long,” said Duffy, who retired a year ago from his career selling electronic components. “I don’t think anybody did, but now the next wave is the economic sanctions, so we’ll see if that works and maybe that is a way for other people to join.”

For others, the war has only reinforced a sense that neither political party is responsive to the needs of voters. 

As he left a tattoo parlor in Ashland, Virginia, 26-year-old Evan Mise said he feels the increase in gas prices and worries about whether his mom will be able to retire or whether he will someday be able to. 

But he had not decided whether to support Democrats or Republicans in November.

“I feel like our government is pretty corrupt through and through,” he said. “It’s kind of just a sit-back-and-watch thing. And I think my generation especially feels helpless.”

Sloan reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Allen G. Breed in Raleigh, N.C., Michael R. Blood in Bakersfield, Calif., Sarah Rankin in Ashland, Va., Jonathan J. Cooper in Scottsdale, Ariz., and Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.

news.title: Stephen Nagy: U.S. trade deal dead until Canada stops being the 'Ugly Ally'
news.text: Under Justin Trudeau, the previous prime minister, Canada’s relationship with its most vital security and trading partner was disastrously mishandled. Cabinet ministers routinely prioritized domestic political points over cross-border diplomacy. We saw Trudeau explicitly campaign against “MAGA conservatism,” while Foreign Affairs Minister Mélanie Joly publicly mused about creating a “game plan” to deal with a hypothetical authoritarian shift in the US. After enjoying dinner and a selfie at Mar-a-Lago following Trump’s 2024 electoral victory, Trudeau flew back to Canada. Just days later, he called Kamala Harris’s electoral defeat a setback for women.
news.author: Special To National Post
